report:
Conclusion: the claim is overstated/misleading for humans. CLA is not a reliable abdominal-fat reducer. The best direct positive signal is an old, small randomized trial in abdominally obese men, but its authors cautioned that sample size and duration were limited and larger trials were needed: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/ . A later 4-week randomized trial explicitly found CLA did **not** reduce visceral fat: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC2129165/ .

For total fat mass, a 2007 human meta-analysis found only a small average effect—about 0.05 kg/week, plateauing over time—so any benefit is clinically minor and not abdominal-specific: https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext . A 2023 dose–response meta-analysis reported small statistically significant improvements overall, but crucially noted that high-quality studies failed to show body-fat-lowering effects: https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366 .

Bottom line: animal and marketing claims exceed human evidence. If CLA does anything, it is a tiny whole-body fat effect, not meaningful targeted belly-fat loss; evidence for reducing abdominal/visceral fat is weak and inconsistent.
